query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, the concentration of Al governs phase stability by promoting the formation of a fine, ordered γ′ (L12) precipitate within an FCC matrix. This dual-phase microstructure retards grain coarsening and detrimental phase transformations under high-temperature, radiation, and environmental exposures while also enabling deformation mechanisms (such as enhanced twinning) that support cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or additively manufactured equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA that, without Al optimization, tends to form a predominantly FCC solid solution that may be unstable under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Systematically modify the Al content (and hence the Al/(Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) ratio) to promote controlled formation of fine γ′ ordered precipitates within the FCC matrix, while keeping processing (e.g., deposition temperature around 800°C) and other elemental concentrations constant.
generation.conditions: Samples produced under controlled DED or casting conditions, aged at high temperatures (around 800°C) to test thermal stability and then subjected to radiation exposures and cryogenic tensile testing. The comparison is made between alloys with optimized Al levels (promoting γ + γ′ dual-phase stability) and a baseline near-equiatomic composition with no engineered precipitate structure.
generation.structural_mediator: The ordered γ′ phase (L12 structure) finely dispersed in the FCC matrix, which acts as a barrier to grain coarsening, solute diffusion, and unwanted phase separation, while also influencing defect interactions during deformation.
generation.mechanism: Al addition increases lattice distortion and encourages local ordering, thereby facilitating the nucleation and stabilization of γ′ precipitates. These precipitates hinder atomic diffusion and retard the transformation to deleterious secondary phases during high-temperature exposure and under irradiation. Simultaneously, the refined microstructure enhances mechanisms such as deformation twinning at cryogenic temperatures, improving toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with an optimized Al concentration should exhibit a higher volume fraction of fine γ′ precipitates, evidenced by a dual-phase (γ + γ′) microstructure. This microstructure is predicted to translate into improved high-temperature strength, enhanced oxidation and radiation resistance (due to slowed diffusion and phase change kinetics), and superior cryogenic toughness compared to the baseline single-phase FCC alloy without γ′ dispersion.
generation.baseline: The baseline is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA produced under the same conditions but without an optimized Al level to deliberately induce a controlled γ′ phase.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to processing conditions (e.g., DED at ~800°C or controlled casting) where diffusion kinetics allow for precipitate formation without excessive coarsening, and within a compositional window where the Al content is neither too low (failing to induce γ′ formation) nor too high (leading to the precipitation of unwanted compounds such as Ni₂AlTi). It is also applicable under service environments ranging from high thermal loads and radiation exposure to cryogenic temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact range of Al concentrations and processing parameters that yield an optimal γ + γ′ microstructure is not fully established. Moreover, while there is supporting evidence for the role of ordered precipitates in related HEA systems, the quantitative contributions of these phases to radiation tolerance and oxidation resistance in this specific alloy system remain to be precisely measured.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni samples where only the Al concentration is varied across a predefined range. Process all samples identically (e.g., via DED at ~800°C) and subject them to identical high-temperature aging, oxidation, irradiation, and cryogenic tensile tests. Use microscopy (XRD, SEM/EBSD) to characterize phase formation, and perform mechanical testing to assess strength, ductility, and toughness across temperatures.
measurements: Phase fraction and size distribution of γ and γ′ phases (using XRD and SEM/EBSD)
High-temperature tensile strength and microhardness measurements
Oxidation resistance (mass gain or scale characterization) under controlled environments
Radiation tolerance indicators (defect density or irradiation-induced hardness changes)
Cryogenic tensile and fracture toughness tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If varying the Al content does not lead to a systematic change in the formation or refinement of γ′ precipitates (i.e., no statistically significant difference in microstructure compared to the baseline) and if the mechanical and environmental performance (high-temperature strength, oxidation/radiation resistance, cryogenic toughness) does not improve relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In particular, the extraordinary ductility and fracture toughness of FCC-structured HEAs at ambient temperature and cryogenic temperatures have garnered significant attention [,,,,]. The low yield strength of FCC-structured HEAs, which is typically just 200 MPa in the as-cast form, is a significant disadvantage, as it is significantly less than the necessary strength of metallic structural materials [,]. To overcome these limitations in mechanical properties, a proposed method is to manufacture an HEA composed of a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix with an ordered FCC structure (L12) precipitated phase, i.e., the γ′ phase, by adding Al + Ti. An HEA based on a γ + γ′ alloy system exhibited excellent thermal stability, coarsening resistance, and strength retention around a temperature of 800 °C [,,,]. The γ′ phase is an ordered phase with an almost exact stoichiometric composition ((Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al)) in the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, with γ′ depending on the Al + Ti content []. Numerous studies have been conducted on the γ′ phase’s formation and mechanical properties [,]. A high content of Al + Ti leads to the formation of precipitate phases such as Ni2AlTi. AbstractThe interface between high-performance thermoelectric materials and electrodes critically governs the conversion efficiency and long-term reliability of thermoelectric generators under high-temperature operation. Here, we propose AlxCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (HEA) as barrier layers to bond Cu-W electrodes with p-type skutterudite (p-SKD) thermoelectric materials. The HEA/p-SKD interface exhibited excellent chemical bonding with a stable and controllable reaction layer, forming a dense, defect-free (Fe,Ni,Co,Cr)Sb phase (thickness of ~2.5 μm) at the skutterudites side. The interfacial resistivity achieved a low value of 0.26 μΩ·cm2 and remained at 7.15 μΩ·cm2 after aging at 773 K for 16 days. Moreover, the interface demonstrated remarkable mechanical stability, with an initial shear strength of 88 MPa. After long-term aging for 16 days at 773 K, the shear strength retained 74 MPa (only 16% degradation), ranking among the highest reported for thermoelectric materials/metal joints.
